1	# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code
2	
3	**seeding**
4	: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
5	
6	**base build**
7	: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.
8	
9	**old code**
10	: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.
11	
12	Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.
13	
14	## Finding or building a base build
15	
16	- If your brief names a base build, use it.
17	- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
18	  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
19	  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
20	  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
21	- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.
22	
23	      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
24	      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
25	      ant compileAll
26	      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
27	      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
28	      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean
29	
30	If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.
31	
32	## Seeding a worktree
33	
34	A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.
35	
36	Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.
37	
38	    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
39	
40	- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
41	- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
42	- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
43	- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
44	- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
45	- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
46	- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
47	- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.
48	
49	## Running the old code
50	
51	If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.
52	
53	`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:
54	
55	    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
56	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
57	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
58	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
59	    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM
60	
61	- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
62	- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
63	- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
64	- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).
65	
66	To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:
67	
68	    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
69	        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss
70	
71	The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".
72

1	# The Claude Code session: the Bash tool, long commands, waits and stops
2	
3	**prompt cache**
4	: API's copy of a conversation's context. It lives five minutes for an agent and one hour for the main session. Each request to the API within that time reads the cache and renews it. The first request after a longer wait writes the whole context again: late in a long task, hundreds of thousands of tokens.
5	
6	**interrupt**
7	: Stop of the session's turn, by the stop button. It kills every agent that runs in the background at that moment, of the Agent tool or of a Workflow.
8	
9	**stop of the process**
10	: End of the session's Claude Code process. It kills every agent. It keeps the conversation, the transcripts and the disk: worktrees, uncommitted edits and logs. A command started with `nohup` (below) survives a stop, but not a restart of the machine.
11	
12	**automatic permission check**
13	: Check that approves each tool call in auto mode. It can refuse a call, also a call that the curator approved in chat.
14	
15	## The Bash tool and waits
16	
17	The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).
18	
19	- In an agent, keep every wait under 240 s.
20	- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.
21	
22	## Long commands
23	
24	If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it detached with `nohup`, after the setup lines, whose exports it inherits. Write the command and the log in the line itself:
25	
26	    nohup bash -c '( ant compileAll ) > tmp/build.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/build.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
27	
28	Keep the setup lines and the `nohup` line as separate lines. `A && nohup B &` runs `A` in the background too, so its `cd` and its exports do not reach the lines after it in the same call.
29	
30	The log gets the output, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`. The automatic permission check refuses a shell function that passes the command to `bash -c` in a variable, because it cannot read the command.
31	
32	The shell function `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 240 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0: ant's `BUILD` and `Total time:`, JUnit's `OK (`, `FAILURES!!!` and `Tests run:`, and `EXIT=`. If not, it returns 1.
33	
34	Run `wait_for` until it returns 0, each time in a new Bash call. Give that call a `timeout` above 240 s, such as 300000 ms: the timeout only guards the call, and `wait_for` itself returns by 240 s. Define the function in each call that uses it. Grep the log for the lines that you need.
35	
36	    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 240]; call again until it returns 0
37	        local n=0 max=${2:-240}
38	        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=240 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 240 ] && max=240
39	        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
40	            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
41	            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
42	        done
43	        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^OK (\|^FAILURES!!!\|^Tests run:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
44	    }
45	
46	If your brief says that you run beside a batch, a run of other agents that build and test at the same time, run every build, suite, stage and program under `nice -n 19`, after `nohup`. Run one command of your own at a time that starts a JVM. The JVMs that it starts count with it.
47	
48	- Start such a command only when the `available` column of `free -g` shows 6 GB or more. If it shows less, check again in each call of a wait, as `wait_for` waits, for at most 30 minutes. If it still shows less, start nothing and report back.
49	- A timed run of the checker is a plain run, under the rules for every other run here; it takes no lock and waits for no other work.
50	
51	## Stopping processes
52	
53	Stop only the processes that run under your tree's path. To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.
54	
55	Kill by process id, with `kill <pid>`. A pattern, as in `pkill -f`, also matches other agents' copies of the same scripts, and your own call's shell, which it then kills.
56	
57	## After an interrupt or a stop of the process
58	
59	If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop of the process:
60	
61	1. Read what is on disk first: `git log` and `git status` in your tree, and your logs.
62	2. If a step's log has ended and the tree has not changed since, the step is done. A log has ended if it has its `EXIT=` line, or its verdict or table is complete.
63	3. If a log has no `EXIT=` line yet, its command may still run. Look for its process under your tree's path. If it runs, wait for it with `wait_for`.
64	4. Continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed.
65	
66	## When the automatic permission check refuses a call
67	
68	- Do not try for the same result with another tool, by another route or in a later turn.
69	- Report the refusal and what was not done because of it. The way through is the curator's: manual approval for the session, or an allow rule for the command (`/permissions`).
70

1	# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild
2	
3	**tree**
4	: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.
5	
6	**library order**
7	: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.
8	
9	**DSL grammar**
10	: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.
11	
12	**parser directory**
13	: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.
14	
15	## Setting up each call
16	
17	Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:
18	
19	    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
20	    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
21	    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
22	    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
23	
24	- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
25	- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
26	- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.
27	
28	The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:
29	
30	- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
31	- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).
32	
33	If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.
34	
35	The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.
36	
37	With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:
38	
39	- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
40	- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.
41	
42	## Two layers of code
43	
44	The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.
45	
46	The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.
47	
48	The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:
49	
50	- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
51	- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
52	- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
53	- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.
54	
55	An edit makes stale what was built from it:
56	
57	- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
58	- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
59	- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
60	- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.
61	
62	## The caches
63	
64	All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:
65	
66	- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
67	- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
68	- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
69	- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).
70	
71	Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).
72	
73	With `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, a run that names no private caches folder uses `default_repository/caches-one` in place of `default_repository/caches`, because a caches folder holds the jars of a single library. Set the environment variable, not only the property `-Dfortress.library=one`. The class path scripts, `bin/fortress_classpath` and `bin/run_classpath`, read only the variable. With the property alone, the compile writes to `caches-one`, but the run looks in `caches` and prints 'Could not load P'. Run the library order without the variable: it fills `caches` with the prelude's jars. A program compiled with the variable runs only if its caches folder holds the jars of the one library's fourteen components, which `one_library_tests/OneLibraryComponents.test` compiles. To fill `caches-one` with them, run that test with `junit.sh` and the variable (`tests-running.md`, "Compiled tests").
74	
75	## The library order
76	
77	The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.
78	
79	Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:
80	
81	- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
82	- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.
83	
84	Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:
85	
86	    cd ProjectFortress
87	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
88	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
89	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
90	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
91	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s
92	
93	Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.
94	
95	- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
96	- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
97	- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.
98	
99	## Name resolution
100	
101	- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
102	- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
103	- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
104	- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
105	- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.
106	
107	## Building
108	
109	Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.
110	
111	- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
112	- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
113	- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` and `default_repository/caches-one`, each if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
114	- `ant cleanCache` deletes both folders, whatever their stamp.
115	- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
116	- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
117	- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.
118	
119	## After an edit of the library
120	
121	The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.
122	
123	- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
124	- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
125	- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
126	- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.
127	
128	## Symptoms of a skipped step
129	
130	If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:
131	
132	- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
133	- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.
134	
135	If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.
136	
137	Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:
138	
139	- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
140	- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.
141	
142	Two more facts help you read a run:
143	
144	- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
145	- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.
146

1	# Writing a test
2	
3	**gated test**
4	: Test that the gate's suites run.
5	
6	**green**
7	: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as passed.
8	
9	**red**
10	: Harness's report on a test that JUnit counts as failed.
11	
12	**`XXX` test**
13	: Gated expected failure. It asserts the answer that the specification gives, and fails today. The harness reports it green while it fails, and red when the defect is fixed.
14	
15	## A test program
16	
17	A test program has this form:
18	
19	    component Name
20	    export Executable
21	
22	    (* declarations *)
23	
24	    run(): () = do
25	        assert(f(2), 4, "f(2)")
26	    end
27	
28	    end
29	
30	- `(*)` starts a comment to the end of the line. It cannot hold `*)`: the parser ends the comment there and refuses the program. `(* ... *)` comments nest.
31	- A compiled test with a `run` key ends `run()` with `println("PASS")`, unless a `run_out` key checks its output (below).
32	- Under walk, `assert(x, y, msg)` checks that `x` equals `y`. It and `=/=` call a type's own `=` only if the type extends a `FortressLibrary` trait that declares `=`, such as `Equality` (ledger row 807). Otherwise they compare by `SEQV` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). If a type `P` has its own `=`, make `P` extend `Equality[\P\]`, or write `assert(x = y, msg)`. The compiler's library declares the two-value `assert` only for `ZZ32`, `String` and `Character`; its `assert(flag, msg)` takes any `Boolean`.
33	- Do not name a variable or a parameter after a functional method of the library, such as `big`, `even`, `numerator` or `shift`. The disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses it: "Variable even is already declared."
34	- A superscript is `^` and what follows it, as the exponent in `x^2` or the transpose `^T`. It can follow a dotted access or a subscript: `p.wq^T` is `(p.wq)^T`, and `x[5]^2` is `(x[5])^2`. After a call, parenthesise first, as `(f(x))^T`: `f(x)^T` is a static error.
35	- A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a variable operand, not a literal, because an expression of literals alone folds before the run (`revival-changes.md`, "Numbers").
36	
37	## Where a test goes, and how it passes
38	
39	Interpreter (walk): write `ProjectFortress/tests/Name.fss`, whose component is `Name`.
40	
41	- Every `.fss` file there is gated, with no `.test` file needed.
42	- It is green if it throws no exception, exits 0, and neither its standard output nor its standard error contains `fail` or `FAIL`. A longer word counts too: `failure` fails the test. Only a file whose name contains `QuickCheckTest` is exempt.
43	- An api that it imports, and a helper component, go in `ProjectFortress/test_library/`. In `tests/`, a helper would run as a test.
44	- The harness skips files whose names end in `Syntax.fss`, `DynamicSemantics.fss` or `Satisfiability.fss`, or contain `GenomeUtil`.
45	- For a refusal at load, put `Name.test` beside `tests/Name.fss`, with `load_exception_contains=<message>`. A plain test is green if walk refuses the program at load as named. A failure while the top-level variables are initialised, or a static error of a phase before the run, such as the disambiguator's, counts as a refusal. An `XXX` test here records a refusal that walk misses: it is green while the program loads and runs clean, and red once walk refuses it.
46	
47	Compiled: write `Name.fss` and `Name.test` in the compiled test folder that holds tests of its kind:
48	
49	- `library_tests/`: the compiler's library. A test of the interpreter's library is an interpreter test (above).
50	- `parser_tests/`: the parser.
51	- `compiler_tests/`: the rest, beside the team's numbered `CompiledN` tests.
52	- `one_library_tests/`: a test whose program compiles against the one library: a test of a binding of the one library, or of a defect that only that library shows. Its tests compile with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`, and `ant testOneLibrary` and `testFast` run them. A plain run test there runs against the one library's jars, as `OneLibraryRunHello.test` does. `compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet", lists what it cannot run, and `tests-running.md`, "Compiled tests", says how to run it.
53	- `other_compiler_tests/`: the team's compiled tests that do not fit the `CompiledN` series. Put no new test there.
54	
55	The `.test` files are the whole list of tests: a `.fss` that no `.test` file names never runs. A `.test` file is a Java property file. It names the commands to run and the checks on their output, as lit's RUN and CHECK lines do:
56	
57	    tests=Name                 the component(s) it drives; without it, the .test file's own name
58	    compile | link | typecheck each present command is one JUnit case; link compiles, then links
59	    run                        run the linked program in a subprocess (bin/fortress run)
60	    <command>_<stream>_<check>=text
61	                               command: compile, link or run; stream: out, err or exception;
62	                               check: contains, does_not_contain, equals, matches,
63	                               WIcontains (containment with runs of whitespace collapsed)
64	
65	A `run` fails if the program exits non-zero or a `run_*` check fails. With no `run_out` check, its output must contain `pass` or `PASS`. With `run_exits_nonzero=true`, the run must exit non-zero, as a program whose class fails to load does. The `run_*` checks, and the `PASS` check where no `run_out` check is given, still apply. For example:
66	
67	    tests=EqualityRung1
68	    link
69	    run
70	    run_out_WIcontains=PASS
71	
72	## How `XXX` works
73	
74	- Under walk, an `XXX` test is `tests/XXXName.fss`, whose component is `XXXName`. With no `.test` file, it is green when it fails as a plain test would.
75	- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name applies to every command that the file drives: each must fail. So a defect at run time, whose link succeeds, needs two `.test` files ("Writing an `XXX` test").
76	- An unmet `run_*` check makes a run test red, whatever the prefix.
77	- The harness reports any link or compile exception of a component whose name contains `XXX` as expected, whatever the `.test` file's name. Only an unmet key of that command makes it red.
78	- An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key, whose program compiles, reports "Saw wrong failure", which is red.
79	- A green `XXX` test prints `Saw expected failure` or `OK Saw expected exception`.
80	
81	## How a defect is recorded
82	
83	Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:
84	
85	1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
86	2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. If walk crashes on the program, still write the `XXX` test, unlike under 3: the harness counts the crash as the expected failure. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
87	3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, or no gated test can pass while it shows, as when walk crashes on the program, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.
88	
89	If your brief does not let you edit the original tree, say in your report which of the three the defect needs, and write a ledger row for it, whichever it needs. The change that next works there writes the test.
90	
91	## The order: the test, its failure, the fix, the pass
92	
93	1. Write the test, with a plain name. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
94	2. Run the test's program through the harness before you run it any other way. In that Bash call, echo a line that starts `Expected failure:` before the harness command. In that line, say how the harness should report the failure. Then see the test fail that way through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build or compile your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. If your tree already holds the fix, run the test through the harness on the old code, as `worktrees.md`, "Running the old code", says. If the test passes, or fails another way, find out why and correct it before you make the fix. Then echo the expected failure again in the Bash call that runs the test again. If the run meets a second defect, record it as "How a defect is recorded" says.
95	3. Make the fix. See the test pass in your last run after your last change of code.
96	
97	The test needs no commit of its own. A test that comes with no fix has no failing run: see it pass through the harness.
98	
99	In your report, quote each `Expected failure:` line as the call echoed it, two to five lines of each failing run, and the passing line, each run with its command. Give the cause of each run that failed another way. In an edit of the original tree, put every check into a gated test, never into a one-off script. A task that only measures may use its own script. Assert a value with `assert` in an interpreter test. In a compiled test, assert it with `assert` (above), or print it and check it with a `run_out_equals` key.
100	
101	An edit of prose in `Specification/` or `Documentation/` has no test. Check it as `specification.md`, "Changing the text: the revision form", says.
102	
103	## Writing an `XXX` test
104	
105	In a compiled test folder, name the component `XXXName`, in its file `XXXName.fss` and in its `component` line.
106	
107	- For a refusal at compile time, write one `XXX` compile test, with `compile` and `compile_err_contains=<the refusal's message>`.
108	- For a code-generator wall (`compiler.md`, "What the compiled path cannot compile yet"), write `XXXName.test` with `tests=XXXName`, `compile` and `compile_exception_contains=<text of the exception>`.
109	- For a program that compiles and fails at run time, write two `.test` files over the component:
110	  - `NameLink.test`, a plain name, with `tests=XXXName` and `link`. It is red if the link reports static errors, but green on an exception.
111	  - `XXXName.test`, with `tests=XXXName` and `run`, and no `link`. Its run uses the plain file's link, so run the two files in one call of `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`, the plain one first.
112	  - The program prints `REACHED` in `run()` before the part that fails. The `XXX` file checks it with `run_out_contains=REACHED`, or with `run_out_does_not_contain=REACHED` if the run dies before `run()` prints. Never use `run_out_contains=PASS`.
113	  - Example: `compiler_tests/XXXBoxDotSpellingsRungW.test` and `BoxDotSpellingsRungWLink.test`.
114	
115	Show the first `XXX` test that your change adds, and only the first, working through the harness (`harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh` or `fortress junit`), from its place in a gated test folder. Run it twice:
116	
117	1. As it is: the harness must report an expected failure.
118	2. Changed for one run so that the defect does not show, then restored: the harness must report it red. For example, add the missing declaration to the test program, set the expected string to what the run prints, or, in a run-time pair, remove the part that fails.

121	
122	If your change fixes a defect that has a gated `XXX` test, the fix turns that test red. To find such a test, search the gap ledger (`records.md`): a row's reproducer names it. Also list the `XXX` files: `git ls-files 'ProjectFortress/*XXX*'`. Then promote it:
123	
124	1. Before you edit the code, remove the prefix: give the test a plain name by its topic. Rename each file with `git mv` (`committing.md` gives the commit), or with `mv` if the file is not committed yet. Rename each `XXX` name inside: the `component` line, and in a compiled test the `tests=` lines and keys. Change a run-time pair as below.
125	2. See the plain-named test fail through the harness on the base's code, as "The order", step 2, says.
126	3. Make the fix and see the test pass.
127	
128	A run-time pair keeps its three files, renamed without `XXX`. For example, `compiler_tests/NatRtTask` was promoted so in `fd5cb4864`:
129	
130	- `Name.fss`, with `component Name`. The program asserts its values, then prints `PASS` last.
131	- `NameLink.test`: `tests=Name` and `link`.
132	- `Name.test`, in place of `XXXName.test`: `tests=Name`, `link`, `run` and `run_out_contains=PASS`.

134	## Names, comments, citations
135	
136	- Name a test by its topic. Give it one comment line that says what it checks, with no pointer to a record.
137	- Assert each case in one test only. Add a new case to the test that already asserts cases of its kind: `git grep` for the case's name or value finds it. A case that fails today goes in an `XXX` test, since it would turn a plain test red.
138	- Write an assertion's message as one short line that says what was checked. Put a reason that several assertions share in one comment line above them.
139	- In a test, cite the specification by file and section or entry, never by line: `opr-overview.tex, subsection "GCD, LCM, and CHOOSE Operators"`. In the library chapters, name the entry too: `basic-integers.tex, section "Integers", opr CHOOSE`.
140	- If your change breaks a line of a test that the team wrote, respell the line and keep the value that it checks. Keep every assertion. List each line's before and after in your report.
141	- If your change touches mutable state, a field, an `atomic` block, library code that writes shared state, or the Java of tasks, transactions or the class loader, run its checks at one thread and at four. `harness-one.sh`, `junit.sh` and the suites force four threads. For one thread, run the program directly with the prefix `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` (a compiled program: `compiler.md`, "Running"), and check its exit code and output.
142	- Under walk, a parallel range of sixteen elements or fewer, as `0#16`, runs its bodies in index order, so a test of parallelism there needs a longer range. For the compiled path, see `compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path".

1	# Running tests
2	
3	**track**
4	: One of the five JVMs of `ant testFast`.
5	
6	**shard**
7	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.
8	
9	**code state**
10	: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.
11	
12	## The two suites
13	
14	`ant testFast` runs its tests in five tracks, four at once, in about 11 minutes:
15	
16	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
17	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
18	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
19	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes, except `OneLibraryJUTest`.
20	- onelibrary: `OneLibraryJUTest` over `one_library_tests/`, with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. It starts when another track ends.
21	
22	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs its tests in four shards, in a few minutes.
23	
24	`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
25	
26	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
27	
28	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
29	
30	The two suites work in the same way:
31	
32	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
33	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
34	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
35	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
36	
37	To run a suite:
38	
39	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
40	- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
41	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
42	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
43	
44	## The switches that the harness reads
45	
46	Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.
47	
48	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
49	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
50	- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
51	- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
52	- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
53	- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.
54	
55	## Outside the gate
56	
57	- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
58	- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
59	  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run, a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`interpreter.md`, "Natives") or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.
60	  - Print the driver with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md#Commands worked out'`. Save the first script that it prints, under "The demo driver", without the text around it, as `tmp/run-demos.sh` in your tree.
61	  - From the tree's root, after you set up the call, run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. It runs long, so run it in the background with a log (`session.md`, "Long commands"). It runs the demos under walk one at a time and writes `tmp/demos/summary.tsv`.
62	  - The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line, must read 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. A demo reaches its end if it exits 0 and its output holds no "fail" in upper or lower case.
63	  - If your change breaks a demo and you know how to repair the demo, repair it in the commit of your change. Otherwise, report the demo, its output and the ledger row that holds the missing feature, as a defect that your change makes or uncovers.
64	- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).
65	
66	## When to run a whole suite
67	
68	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
69	- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk, of a phase that both paths share or of such a class under `nativeHelpers/`, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
70	  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
71	  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
72	  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`), the parser or such a class, run both.
73	- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
74	- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
75	- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the runtime (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
76	- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests. After an edit of one of the fourteen components that `OneLibraryComponents.test` compiles, also run `ant testOneLibrary` (`library.md`, "Designing a change").
77	
78	The suites do not check these:
79	
80	- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
81	- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
82	- the linker's aliasing of apis;
83	- `fortress unparse`;
84	- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
85	- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.
86	
87	If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.
88	
89	## One test, or a few
90	
91	Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.
92	
93	### Interpreter tests
94	
95	Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:
96	
97	    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
98	        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]
99	
100	- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
101	- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
102	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
103	- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
104	- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
105	- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
106	- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.
107	
108	To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:
109	
110	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss
111	
112	The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").
113	
114	### Compiled tests
115	
116	Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`). The tests of `one_library_tests/` compile against the one library, and a run test there needs the jars of its fourteen components. Run the tests in one of these ways:
117	
118	- `ant testOneLibrary` compiles the fourteen first, with `OneLibraryComponents.test`, in its own caches folder, `ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary`. Each suite deletes that folder when it starts, and only `testFast` and `testOneLibrary` fill it again.
119	- With `junit.sh`, set `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ONE_JVM=1`, and name `OneLibraryComponents.test` first. The compiles write to `default_repository/caches-one`, and the jars stay there after the call. Its `FortressLibrary` alone takes about 135 to 160 s, so run the call in the background (`session.md`).
120	- For a run by hand against the onelibrary track's jars, set `FORTRESS_CACHES=<tree>/ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary` and `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. The build does not touch that folder, so run `ant testOneLibrary` again after an edit of Java or Scala.
121	
122	The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.
123	
124	    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
125	        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1
126	
127	- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
128	- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
129	- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
130	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
131	- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
132	- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

134	To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:

136	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test

138	Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- A probe is a task of a brief that builds a change to answer a question and does not land it. Commit its change as a patch file, with its report and programs, in the `probes/` folder that the brief names, and no edit of the original tree. If the brief names no folder, commit nothing of the probe: give the patch's path and the report in your final message.
13	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
14	- Do not commit `.claude/worktrees/` or `.claude/agents/`, which show as untracked in a fresh clone.
15	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, also gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
16	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
17	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
18	
19	## How to commit
20	
21	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
22	
23	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
24	
25	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
26	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
27	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
28	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
29	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
30	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
31	
32	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
33	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
34	
35	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
36	
37	## Pushing
38	
39	Push after every commit.

221	- The **prelude** is the small library that the compiled path uses today. The **one library** is the interpreter's library. At the **switch-over**, the compiled path moves onto the one library and the prelude is deleted.

226	- **Dispatch** is the choice of which declaration of an overloaded name a call runs. A **functional method** is a method called like a function, `f(x)`, with `self` among its parameters, not always first.
227	- An **atomic block** runs as one transaction: other tasks see all of its writes or none. A **label** block can be left early by an **exit**.
228	- A **numeral** is a number as written, such as `00.5`. A program's own number type takes a numeral through a **coercion** that reads the numeral's four numbers, among them its count of digits.

#!/bin/bash
# seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
#
# Makes a worktree that is ready to compile and run Fortress without building anything, by copying the
# build and the caches of a baseline worktree that has been built once, and translating the parts of the
# caches that are keyed by the source tree's absolute path (explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md).
#
#   <base-worktree>  a clean worktree of this repository at some commit B, on which `ant compileAll` and the
#                    library-order recompile (explorations/repo-internals.md, "Compile order matters") have
#                    run, and nothing since.
#   <new-worktree>   where the new worktree goes; made by `git worktree add`, reused if it already exists.
#   <branch>         the branch it checks out: an existing local branch, else origin's, else a new branch
#                    cut from <start-point>, which defaults to B; `-` makes a detached worktree at
#                    <start-point> instead. Old-against-new runs need no copy of the base: tools/old-fortress.sh
#                    runs the base build itself with a private caches folder.
#
# What it does, in order: adds the worktree; copies ProjectFortress/build, ProjectFortress/.dependencies
# and default_repository/caches from the base; renames every file of the AST caches (analyzed_cache,
# interpreter_cache, interpreter_parsed_cache) to the hash of its source's new path (NamingCzar.deCaseName,
# compiler/NamingCzar.java:244-245; GraphNode.java:33 hashes the canonical path) and rewrites the base path
# inside it; rewrites the base path in the bytecode-cache jars' SourceFile attributes (debug information
# only: jars copied unchanged also run, but their stack traces would name the base's files); and makes the
# new worktree the base's replica in its file dates too. The copies keep the base's dates (cp -a), every
# tracked file whose content is the base's takes the base file's date, and every tracked file that differs
# from B, committed or not, is stamped later than everything copied. Dates decide three things. The
# repository uses a cached entry only when it is not older than its source (repository/GraphRepository.java:244,
# :283; a changed api also makes everything that imports it stale, :600-620). Ant regenerates the AST
# nodes, the parsers and Operators.java when an input is newer than the generated file (build.xml:371-384,
# :450-467, :1335-1400); the checkout's own dates make it regenerate them, and javac then recompiles 1,077
# files. And javac recompiles a source newer than its class (build-cache-exploration.md, section 6). So the
# next `fortress compile` of a differing library source rebuilds it, and a worktree whose ProjectFortress/src
# differs from B is seeded with a warning: the copied build is B's, so the worker runs ant compileAll, which
# recompiles the differing sources (and deletes the caches, build.xml:715 and :356), and the library-order
# recompile before its first compiled run. The base's own dates must be a build's: a base built in place by
# ant, or seeded by this script.
#
# A worktree that already has ProjectFortress/build is left alone (a relaunch keeps the worker's own build);
# SEED_FORCE=1 replaces its build and caches with the base's.
#
# Prints one line per step with its time, and the seeded worktree's path last. Exits non-zero, having
# removed nothing, if the base is not built or not clean. Never touches the base or the main tree.
# Run it from anywhere; it needs bash, git, python3, realpath and bc.
set -euo pipefail

BASE_ARG=${1:?usage: seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]}
NEW_ARG=${2:?new worktree path}
BRANCH=${3:?branch}
BASE=$(realpath "$BASE_ARG")
step () { local now; now=$(date +%s.%N); printf '%-34s %5.1f s\n' "$1" "$(echo "$now - $T" | bc)"; T=$now; }
T=$(date +%s.%N); T_START=$T

# The base must be built and clean, or its caches do not describe its commit.
for f in ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class \
         default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar \

#!/bin/bash
# harness-one.sh <scratch-dir> <file.fss>... : rung C's harness-one.sh (explorations/compile-ladder/
# rung-interp-coercion/, itself rung I's shape): the testSystem harness (SystemJUTest, the class build.xml's
# testSystem shards run) over a directory holding only the named test files, with the JVM settings of
# build.xml's systemShard macro and a private cache. Run from FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh.
#
# The scratch directory is deleted when the call starts and when it ends. The private cache is the folder
# <scratch-dir>.cache beside it, kept between calls. A call starts from what that folder holds when it was
# filled under the implementation now built (ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp, which ant compileAll
# writes) and from the Fortress sources now on the source path outside the scratch directory (the .fss and
# .fsi files of Library, ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin, ProjectFortress/test_library and ProjectFortress);
# otherwise it empties the folder first. COLD_CACHE=1 empties it in any case. The folder is stamped only when
# the JVM ends normally, so a call that is killed leaves it to be emptied by the next one.
set -u
S=$(realpath -m -- "${1:?scratch dir}") ; shift
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:?}
C=$S.cache
BUILT=$FH/ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp
sources_key () {
    ( cd "$FH" && { find Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin ProjectFortress/test_library -type f -name '*.fs[si]' -print0
                    find ProjectFortress -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.fs[si]' -print0 ; } \
        | sort -z | xargs -0 -r sha1sum | sha1sum | cut -c1-40 )
}
key () { [ -f "$BUILT" ] && echo "$(head -1 "$BUILT") sources $(sources_key)" ; }
rm -rf "$S" ; mkdir -p "$S/tests" "$S/tmp"
KEY=$(key)
if [ -z "${COLD_CACHE:-}" ] && [ -n "$KEY" ] && [ "$(cat "$C/harness.stamp" 2>/dev/null)" = "$KEY" ]; then
    CACHE=filled
else
    rm -rf "$C" ; mkdir -p "$C" ; printf '\0\0\0\0' > "$C/global.map" ; CACHE=empty
fi
rm -f "$C/harness.stamp"
for f in "$@" ; do cp "$f" "$S/tests/" ; done
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
echo "# harness-one $(date -u +%FT%TZ); tree $(git -C "$FH" rev-parse --short HEAD); nproc=$(nproc); load $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=4; cache $CACHE"
cd "$FH/ProjectFortress" && FORTRESS_THREADS=4 FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1 FORTRESS_CACHES="$C" \
  java -Xmx768m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir="$S/tmp" -Dfortress.caches="$C" -Dtests="$S/tests" \
       -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.tests.unit_tests.SystemJUTest 2>&1 | grep -v '^\s*at ' | sed "s#$FH/##g"
RC=${PIPESTATUS[0]}
echo "exit=$RC"

content.content:
## The site

- In a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, the checker types `self` as the trait met with them, a `TraitSelfType` read as `QQ & Ratio` in a subtype test (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala:185`, `:579-586`), as the specification gives (`Specification/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex:63-69`). It reads the `self` parameter of `QQ`'s own declaration the same way, so `QQ`'s `denominator(self)` and `Ratio`'s have equivalent domains and neither is more specific (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/CoercionOracle.scala:77-78`).
- A tie among candidates that fit the call as it is kept the sort's head (`Functionals.scala:1103-1108` before the fix). The sort keeps the input order where neither precedes (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/PartialOrder.scala:53`). The input is the call's overloadings (`Functionals.scala:1638`), in the order of the disambiguator's `toSet(env.unambiguousFunctionNames(...)).toList` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/disambiguator/ExprDisambiguator.scala:431`, `:482`), which iterates the index's set of `Function`s (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/disambiguator/TopLevelEnv.java:465-466`). No class under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/index/` overrides `hashCode`, so that order follows the JVM's identity hashes (F-232). Ledger row 935 records this order; row 1100 records this tie's failure.
- The function reference takes the head's arrow (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1249-1253`), and the code generator writes the call's descriptor from it (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1783`).

By run, with copies of `Functionals.scala` compiled into scratch folders and put first on the class path (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/compiler.md`, "Testing an edit here"), never in the tree:

- an instrumented copy printed the tie at all 38 calls of `numerator` and `denominator` on `self` in `QQ`'s bodies, for example `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:641:47-49 top=(QQ & {Ratio})->ZZ | Ratio->ZZ atSelf=(QQ & {Ratio})->ZZ sortedHead=(QQ & {Ratio})->ZZ`, and no case where a candidate that takes `self` at its trait's type lost to a strictly more specific one;
- a copy that reverses `denominator`'s overloadings, putting `Ratio`'s first, reproduced the gate's failure in a one-JVM run: '. run one_library_tests/OneLibraryRunHello (598ms) Exception in thread "main" java.lang.VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack', the 14 `denominator` calls at `Ratio`;
- the same reversed copy with the fix gave the 14 calls at `QQ` and 'Hello, one library', 'OK (16 tests)'.

## The repair

A tie that `self`'s type makes keeps, of the tied candidates, those that take each argument with `self` read as its trait alone, where some but not all do; the sort's head among them is the call's head. Any other tie keeps the sort's head as before. `QQ`'s declaration takes `self` at `QQ`; `Ratio`'s does not, so `QQ`'s is the head whatever the order: the call compiles at `QQ`'s arrow, the value that the compiled call passes, and at run time dispatch reaches `Ratio`'s body, as `Specification/basic/overloading.tex`, "Overloading Resolution", gives.

Ways not taken:

- The order of `TopLevelEnv.unambiguousFunctionNames` sorted by the declarations' spans. It changes the head of every tie of every call in the compiled path, the generic ties of rows 499, 1046 and 1047 among them, whose gated tests were written against today's behaviour. The remaining orders are the judge's third item for the curator.
- The candidates restricted to those that take `self` at its trait's type wherever one does. It would also change calls where a listed type's declaration is strictly more specific, which the specification selects statically (`var-ref.tex:63-69`), and it changes the call's static type there. The instrumented copy found no such call in the one library.
- The specification's own static choice kept, `Ratio`'s declaration, made free of the order, with the code generator casting `self` at the call as F-377 describes. Two changes, one in `CodeGen.java`; and the call would still name the overload method that row 815 finds missing.

## Tests

- The nine `one_library_tests` run tests, unchanged. Before the fix, `ant testOneLibrary` from 13:31Z: '[junit] Tests run: 40, Failures: 9, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0, Time elapsed: 204.252 sec', 'BUILD FAILED'. After: '[junit] Tests run: 40, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0, Time elapsed: 195.958 sec', 'BUILD SUCCESSFUL'.
- `ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall`, a trait that comprises one object, with four abstract functional methods, a getter `total` that calls them on `self`, and a getter `kind` that the run calls, which loads the trait's default methods. On the merged code before the fix, under the hash flag, by `../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall.test` with a private copy of the prelude's caches:

      Expected failure: on the merged code before the fix, under -XX:hashCode=0, ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall's run dies as Solid's default methods load, 'VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack ... not assignable to ...Brick'
      . run compiler_tests/ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall (229ms) java.lang.VerifyError
          ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall$Solid$DefaultTraitMethods.total(LComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall$Solid;)Lcom/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32; @1: invokestatic
          Type 'ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall$Solid' (current frame, stack[0]) is not assignable to 'ComprisesSelfAbstractFunctionalMethodCall$Brick'

  In the default hash mode, through `ONE_JVM=1 .../climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`, it passed before the fix, 'OK (3 tests)': that JVM's order put `Solid`'s declarations first. After the fix, through `junit.sh` and under the flag by hand: 'OK (3 tests)' both, '. run ... PASS'.
- The S and O tests that the ruling names, `ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh SO ProjectFortress/compiler_tests` with the four `FunctionalMethod*` pairs, the `OverrideModifierCodeGeneration` pair and the seven `XXXOverride*` files: 'OK (22 tests)'.
- `Functionals`' largest method after the change is 5250 bytes of bytecode (`checkExprFunctionals`), under `MethodSizeJUTest`'s 8,000.

## Deviations from the ruling

1. Step 1 expected the `VerifyError` from a one-JVM compile in the way `tests-running.md:119` gives. That run, and the same under the hash flag, compiled `QQ`'s calls at `QQ` and ran 'Hello, one library'; the failure reproduced only in ant's onelibrary JVM (the runs above). Row 1100 had recorded the same: `Ratio` "when `FortressLibrary` compiles after other programs in one JVM", `QQ` "compiled first in a fresh JVM".
2. Step 3's test did not flip either build by the flag. Its condition for step 4 held all the same, the merged code under the flag making the base's call, and the one build disagreed with itself between JVMs, which no rung's logic can do; so step 3's bisect did not run.
3. Step 4's premise, that `Ratio`'s declaration is not applicable at the arguments' static types, is wrong against the specification: in a trait with a `comprises` clause `self` has the type `T ∩ (U1 ∪ … ∪ Un)` (`Specification/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex:63-69`), so `Ratio`'s `denominator(self)` is applicable at `self`'s static type. With `QQ`'s declaration at `QQ` (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:609`), the specification's static choice is the more specific, `Ratio`'s (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:355-358`). The checker reads `QQ`'s own `self` parameter as the same meet, so it ties the two, and no iteration picks between them by a rule. The repair makes the tie's choice free of the order as "The repair" says. The call's static type at such a tie is the head's return type, `QQ`'s; where a listed type's declaration returns a strictly narrower type, the specification gives the narrower. (* A value typed by a trait stands, compiled, where a type that the trait's comprises clause lists is expected: as an argument of a function, a method and a constructor, as a returned value, at a typed binding and at an assignment. *)
component ComprisesValueAtListedTypeCompiled
export Executable

trait Q comprises { R }
    getter fin(): Boolean = (den(self) > 0)
    numBy(t: Taker): ZZ32 = t.num(self)
    both(): ZZ32 = sum(self, self)
    listed(): R = self
    bound(): ZZ32 = do
        r: R = self
        r.d
      end
    assigned(): ZZ32 = do
        var r: R = R(0, 0)
        r := self
        r.d
      end
    held(): ZZ32 = Holder(self).r.d
    kept[\T extends Object\](x: T): R = self
    cased(): R = typecase self of
        r: R => self
      end
end

value object R(n: ZZ32, d: ZZ32) extends Q end

den(r: R): ZZ32 = r.d
sum(a: R, b: R): ZZ32 = a.n + b.d

object Taker
    num(r: R): ZZ32 = r.n
end

object Holder(r: R) end

trait Shape comprises { Disc, Square }
    area(): ZZ32 = typecase self of
        c: Disc => discArea(c)
        q: Square => squareArea(q)
      end
end

object Disc(r: ZZ32) extends Shape end
object Square(s: ZZ32) extends Shape end

discArea(c: Disc): ZZ32 = 3 c.r c.r
squareArea(q: Square): ZZ32 = q.s q.s

run(): () = do
    q: Q = R(1, 2)
    assert(q.fin, "a function's argument")
    assert(q.numBy(Taker), 1, "a method's argument")
    assert(q.both(), 3, "two arguments")
    assert(q.listed().d, 2, "a returned value")
    assert(q.bound(), 2, "a typed binding")
    assert(q.assigned(), 2, "an assignment")
    assert(q.held(), 2, "a value parameter")
    assert(q.kept[\ZZ32\](7).d, 2, "a returned value of a generic method")
    assert(q.cased().d, 2, "a returned typecase whose arm is self")
    d: Shape = Disc(2)
    s: Shape = Square(5)
    assert(d.area(), 12, "the first listed type after a typecase")
    assert(s.area(), 25, "the second listed type after a typecase")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

aplFloor[\nat s\](v: Vector[\RR64,s\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] =
    v.map[\RR64\](fn (x: RR64): RR64 => 1.0 (|\ x /|))

(* ---------------------------------------------- ≡ match, ≢ tally/notmatch - *)
(* ≡ and ≢ are in the host table (EQV, NEQV) and take both arities.  APL's
   match compares shape first, so the cross-rank cases are separate overloads:
   six of them for three ranks, the price of putting rank in the type. *)
opr ≡(a: RR64, b: RR64): RR64 = if a = b then 1.0 else 0.0 end
opr ≡[\nat s, nat t\](a: Vector[\RR64,s\], b: Vector[\RR64,t\]): RR64 =
    if |a| =/= |b| then 0.0
    elif |a| = 0 then 1.0

%  opr EQV(self, other: Boolean): Boolean
%  opr =(self, other: Boolean): Boolean
%  opr IFF(self, other: Boolean): Boolean
\Method{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\equiv}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \TYP{Boolean})\COLON \TYP{Boolean}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{=}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \TYP{Boolean})\COLON \TYP{Boolean}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\leftrightarrow}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \TYP{Boolean})\COLON \TYP{Boolean}}}

The logical equivalence, or exclusive \scap{nor}, operator \EXP{\equiv} (\STR{EQV}) returns \VAR{true} if
both arguments are \VAR{true} or both arguments are \VAR{false}; it returns \VAR{false} if
the arguments are different, one being \VAR{true} and the other \VAR{false}.
(Thus its behavior on boolean values happens to be exactly the same as that of the strict equivalence operator \EXP{\sequiv}.)

The equality operator \EXP{=} and the if-and-only-if operator \EXP{\leftrightarrow} (\STR{IFF}) do the same thing as \EXP{\equiv}.

For \EXP{\not\equiv} \see{operator-NEQV}.
For \EXP{\neq} \see{operator-NE}.

  opr OPLUS(self, other:Boolean):Boolean
  opr NEQV(self, other:Boolean):Boolean

content.content:
- F-377 **The compiled code casts `self` where the checker reads it as a listed type or as the self-type parameter.** `CodeGen.castToTypeBelow` casts a value that has self's type (the checker's `TraitSelfType` with a non-empty list: a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, or a trait with a sel
f-type parameter) to a declared trait type or type variable strictly below its trait. It casts at the argument of a call with one argument (a call with several arguments casts each already), at a typed binding and an assignment, at a method's returned value, at each arm of a conditional or a `case` 
expression, at the conditional's type, and at a function expression's and a local function's result, also where the value is a typecase whose arms each have self's type. So `den(self)` for `den(r: R)` in `trait Q comprises { R }`, `twin(self): S = self` and `mx(self, other: T): T = if lt(other, self
) then self else other end` in a self-typed trait verify and run (rows 991, 695, 1050 and 1051, fixed), as the one library's `QQ comprises { Ratio }` and `StandardTotalOrder`'s `MIN` and `MAX` need. A conditional or typecase whose arms are pairs that hold `self`, `MINMAX`'s shape, verifies and runs 
with no cast, since the declared tuple type is a JVM interface and the caller converts the result; a typecase whose arms are all `self` has a one-element union, which is cast.
